name: New Caledonia
summary_text: New Caledonia is a French collectivity in which France retains responsibility for penal law, civil-status documents and the justice system, while New Caledonia legislates locally on many domestic matters. The protections a trans visitor would rely on are French national provisions that apply here as French law, and no source in this inventory records a local ordinance narrowing them. Nothing in the inventory criminalises trans people or same-sex relations.  Same-sex marriage has been available in New Caledonia since France's 2013 marriage-equality statute, which applies here as French law. CNN reported on 29 May 2013 on the first same-sex wedding solemnised in France under that law. PinkNews reported on 26 August 2012 that the French government would introduce its same-sex marriage and adoption bill into Parliament in October 2012, fulfilling President Hollande's campaign pledge.  Sexual identity became a ground of discrimination in the French Penal Code through the sexual-harassment legislation of 2012, which enabled prosecution of discrimination and of transphobia as discrimination. Yagg reported that change in July 2012; the provision was amended in 2016 to read gender identity. As French law, the provision reaches New Caledonia.  Placement of detainees follows the recorded legal gender marker rather than anatomy. Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code assigns incarcerated trans people according to their recorded sex, which in practice puts trans women in all-male facilities where they face threats of assault by other detainees. BuzzFeed News reported that practice on 12 January 2018. The French prison framework governs the collectivity's establishments in the same way.  France's detention-places watchdog, the CGLPL, issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 finding a persistence of serious violations of the rights of transgender detainees across all French places of deprivation of liberty. Its findings rest on referrals made since 2010 concerning some forty transgender people and on inspections at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse, where eight trans women and one trans man were interviewed. Because French law applies here, the opinion extends to establishments in New Caledonia.

name: Niger
summary_text: Niger State stands under Nigeria's national framework, which reaches into every part of the state. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 criminalises same-sex conduct nationwide and extends well beyond marriage: Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that it also bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with penalties of 10 to 14 years' imprisonment, and that police have used it to justify torture and arbitrary arrests. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment.  A second, state-level layer applies in Niger State specifically. Human Rights Watch (2004) documents the wave of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria and lists the twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The wave traces from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated 27 October 1999 and in force 27 January 2000, and the provisions remain in force. The UK Home Office note records Sharia law in all twelve states as criminalising same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions.  Niger State enacted its own statutory machinery for that layer. The Penal Code (Amendment) Law 2000 (HB.4/2000) was signed into law on 22 February 2000 and came into operation on 4 May 2000, gazetted as Niger State Gazette Vol. 25 No. 8 of 9 March 2000 (pp. B29-B36). It is a law to amend Penal Code Law Cap 94, Laws of Niger State, to review the punishments therein. The enactment defines adultery to include sodomy and inserts section 68A, under which a Muslim convicted of a listed offence and proved against him to the Islamic evidentiary standard receives the harsher punishment specified by Sharia, with amputation added to the caning paragraph of section 68; the ordinary Penal Code punishment otherwise applies.  The editor of Ostien's sourcebook notes that the 2000 enactment is not a complete Sharia Penal Code. It amends the Penal Code of 1960 so that certain sections, applied to Muslims, carry different burdens of proof and different punishments than when applied to non-Muslims, and the text is reproduced in full. The UK Home Office note sets out Nigeria's hybrid legal system, the twelve-state Sharia criminal layer and its coverage of women.  The consequence for a visitor is a parallel track that operates independently of federal law. A Muslim visitor who is outed in Niger State stands under a harsher legal frame than the national statute alone imposes, because religion and the standard of proof determine which punishment applies to the same conduct. The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice for Nigeria, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

sources.title: Niger New Penal Code (February 2026, marriage provisions June 2026)
sources.documents: Sanctions 5-10 years prison + fine up to 100M CFA for same-sex relations, public announcement of same-sex relationship, and changing or attempting to change one's birth sex; 10-20 years + fine up to 500M CFA for creating/managing/financing/participating in LGBTQIA+ organizations/clubs/venues; no mitigating circumstances or suspended sentences
sources.detail: Cited as new penal code adopted February 2026, marriage sanctions effective June 2026; no URL visible in text
